title: Smoky Tomato Shrimp & Cheddar Grits
dek: Plump paprika shrimp sit over buttery sharp-cheddar grits with a quick garlicky tomato pan sauce—Southern comfort with enough acidity to stay lively.
image_alt: Seared shrimp over creamy cheddar grits with a chunky red tomato sauce, black pepper, and tender microgreens in a white bowl
ingredients: 1 lb large raw shrimp (21 to 25 count), peeled and deveined, tails optional
1 tbsp plus 1 tsp olive oil, divided
1 cup stone-ground yellow or white grits (not instant)
4 oz sharp cheddar, finely grated (about 1 cup)
1 can (14.5 oz) fire-roasted diced tomatoes, drained with 1/3 cup juices reserved
2 tsp fresh lemon juice, plus wedges for serving
1 packed cup tender microgreens or baby arugula, optional

instructions.name: Dry and season the shrimp
instructions.text: Pat the shrimp very dry. Toss with the smoked paprika, 1/4 teaspoon kosher salt, cayenne if using, and 1 teaspoon olive oil. Leave at room temperature only while the grits start, no longer than 20 minutes.

instructions.name: Start the stone-ground grits
instructions.text: Bring 3 1/2 cups broth to a boil in a heavy 3-quart saucepan. Whisk in the grits in a thin stream. Reduce the heat to low and cook, partially covered, for 20 to 25 minutes, whisking every 3 to 4 minutes and scraping the corners, until tender and creamy. Add splashes of the remaining 1/2 cup broth if they tighten before becoming tender.

instructions.name: Finish the cheddar grits
instructions.text: Whisk in the milk and 1 tablespoon butter. Remove from the heat, fold in the cheddar a handful at a time, and season with 1/4 teaspoon salt. Cover to keep warm; loosen with warm broth or milk just before serving because stone-ground grits thicken as they stand.

instructions.name: Sear to safe doneness
instructions.text: While the grits cook, heat a 12-inch skillet over medium-high until a drop of water sizzles. Add 1 tablespoon olive oil and the shrimp in one uncrowded layer. Sear for 60 to 90 seconds per side, just until opaque and 145°F in the thickest shrimp. Transfer immediately to a clean plate so carryover heat does not make them rubbery.

instructions.name: Build the smoky tomato sauce
instructions.text: Lower the skillet to medium. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon butter and the garlic; stir for 30 seconds. Add the drained tomatoes, reserved tomato juice, Worcestershire, and remaining 1/4 teaspoon salt. Scrape up the browned paprika bits and simmer for 4 to 5 minutes, until glossy rather than watery.

instructions.name: Return, brighten, and plate
instructions.text: Return the shrimp and any juices to the sauce for 30 seconds, just to rewarm. Remove from the heat and stir in lemon juice. Spoon the cheddar grits into warm bowls, add the tomato shrimp, and finish with scallions, microgreens if using, black pepper, and lemon wedges.

why_it_works: Whisking grits into fully boiling broth prevents clumps, while low heat and periodic scraping hydrate the grain without scorching it.
Searing the shrimp separately concentrates the smoky seasoning and lets you remove them at 145°F before the tomato sauce reduces.
Sharp cheddar supplies savory depth, while fire-roasted tomatoes and lemon cut through the richness of the butter, milk, and cheese.
swaps: Use regular old-fashioned grits and follow their package timing; do not substitute instant grits, which need far less liquid and cook too quickly for this method.
For pescatarian cooking, use low-sodium vegetable or seafood broth and replace Worcestershire with a vegetarian Worcestershire sauce.
Replace shrimp with 1 lb dry-packed sea scallops; sear in two batches and cook to 145°F without simmering them in the sauce.
storage: Refrigerate the shrimp sauce and grits in separate shallow airtight containers for up to 3 days. Reheat grits over low heat with 2 to 4 tablespoons broth or milk per serving, stirring until steaming. Reheat the shrimp sauce gently to 165°F only once; hard boiling will toughen the shrimp. Freezing is not recommended.
notes: The full recipe takes about 45 minutes: 15 minutes prep and 30 minutes cooking. Stone-ground grits vary, so use texture—not only the clock—as the endpoint.
Finely grated cheese melts smoothly. Pre-shredded cheese often contains anti-caking starch that can make the grits slightly grainy.
The calorie and cost estimates include the optional greens but not toast or other side dishes.

faqs.a: The grits were likely added too quickly or not whisked during the first minute. Bring the liquid to a full boil, rain in the grits slowly while whisking, then whisk firmly; small lumps can usually be pressed against the pan and dispersed.
Yes. Thaw them overnight in the refrigerator or under cold running water, then drain and pat completely dry. Wet shrimp steam, dilute the paprika seasoning, and leave the pan sauce thin.

faqs.q: How can I make the dish less rich?
faqs.a: Use 2% milk, reduce cheddar to 3 ounces, and omit the finishing butter in the grits. Keep the lemon and tomatoes at full strength so the bowl remains balanced.

title: Creamy Mushroom Risotto with Parmesan & Parsley
dek: Deeply browned mushrooms crown glossy Arborio rice finished with Parmesan, butter, parsley, and lemon—an attainable vegetarian dinner with restaurant-level texture.
image_alt: Creamy mushroom risotto topped with browned sliced mushrooms, finely shredded Parmesan, chopped parsley, and black pepper on a white plate
ingredients: 1 lb cremini mushrooms, wiped clean and sliced 1/4 inch thick
1 small yellow onion, finely diced (about 1 cup)
1/2 cup dry white wine, or additional broth
3/4 cup finely grated Parmesan, plus more for serving

instructions.name: Keep the broth hot
instructions.text: Bring the vegetable broth to a bare simmer in a medium saucepan, then keep it hot over low heat. Hot broth maintains a steady, gentle simmer when it meets the rice; cold broth repeatedly stalls cooking and can leave the grains uneven.

instructions.name: Brown the mushrooms in batches
instructions.text: Heat a wide 5- to 6-quart Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 tablespoon olive oil and half the mushrooms in one layer. Season with 1/4 teaspoon salt and cook without stirring for 3 minutes, then toss until browned, 2 minutes more. Transfer to a plate and repeat with 1 tablespoon oil, the remaining mushrooms, another 1/4 teaspoon salt, and 1/4 teaspoon pepper.

instructions.name: Sweat the aromatics
instructions.text: Reduce the pot to medium. Add the remaining 1 tablespoon oil and onion; cook for 4 minutes until translucent but not browned. Add garlic and stir for 30 seconds. Add the Arborio rice and toast for 2 minutes, stirring, until the grains smell nutty and their edges look translucent.

instructions.name: Deglaze and begin ladling
instructions.text: Pour in the wine and stir until almost fully absorbed, about 2 minutes. Add the thyme and 3/4 cup hot broth. Maintain a lively but not violent simmer and stir every 20 to 30 seconds until the pan looks nearly dry before adding the next 3/4 cup.

instructions.name: Cook to a flowing texture
instructions.text: Continue adding hot broth in 3/4-cup portions for 20 to 25 minutes. Begin tasting after 18 minutes. The rice is ready when each grain is tender with a faint firm core and the risotto spreads slowly when spooned onto a plate. You may not need the final 1/2 cup broth, or you may need a splash of hot water.

instructions.name: Mantecare off the heat
instructions.text: Remove the pot from the heat. Vigorously stir in Parmesan, cold butter, lemon zest, lemon juice, half the parsley, remaining 3/4 teaspoon salt, and remaining 1/4 teaspoon pepper. Fold in half the mushrooms. Cover and rest for exactly 2 minutes, then loosen with hot broth if it no longer flows.

instructions.name: Finish with the browned mushrooms
instructions.text: Divide immediately among four warm shallow bowls. Top with the reserved browned mushrooms, remaining parsley, extra finely grated Parmesan, and black pepper. Risotto should be served promptly; it continues absorbing liquid as it waits.

why_it_works: Browning mushrooms in uncrowded batches drives off their water and builds caramelized flavor instead of steaming them into the rice.
Gradual additions of hot broth plus frequent—not frantic—stirring release enough Arborio starch for creaminess while preserving distinct grains.
Finishing with cold butter and Parmesan away from direct heat emulsifies the liquid and fat into the signature glossy, flowing texture.
swaps: Use a mix of cremini, shiitake, and oyster mushrooms, keeping the total weight at 1 lb and slicing dense stems thinly.
Omit wine and deglaze with 1/2 cup hot broth plus 1 teaspoon lemon juice; the finished risotto will still have balancing acidity.
For a dairy-free version, use 3 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil in place of the butter and a dairy-free Parmesan alternative; adjust salt after adding it.
storage: Cool leftovers quickly in a shallow container and refrigerate for up to 3 days. Reheat over medium-low heat with 1/4 cup broth per serving, stirring until it reaches 165°F. The rice will be softer than freshly made. Do not leave cooked rice at room temperature longer than 2 hours; freezing noticeably changes the texture.
notes: The realistic total is about 55 minutes: 15 minutes prep and 40 minutes cooking. Broth absorption varies with pan width, heat, and rice brand.
Do not rinse Arborio rice; its surface starch is essential to the creamy sauce.
Use a microplane-style grater for Parmesan so it melts quickly without forming stringy clumps.

faqs.q: Why did my risotto turn gluey?
faqs.a: It was probably cooked too hard, stirred constantly, or held too long after finishing. Maintain a gentle simmer, stir at short intervals rather than nonstop, stop when the center is barely firm, and serve immediately.

faqs.q: Can I make risotto ahead for guests?
faqs.a: You can par-cook it for about 13 minutes using roughly half the broth, spread it on a sheet pan to cool quickly, and refrigerate for up to 1 day. Finish with hot broth, then add butter, cheese, lemon, and mushrooms just before serving.

faqs.q: What if I run out of broth before the rice is tender?
faqs.a: Switch to hot water in 1/2-cup additions. The rice already holds plenty of seasoning, and using water is better than forcing undercooked grains or adding cold liquid.

title: Burnt Basque Cheesecake with Vanilla & Lemon
dek: A deeply bronzed, parchment-crinkled top gives way to a custardy vanilla-lemon center—dramatic enough for company and deliberately free of a fussy crust.
image_alt: Thick slice of crustless burnt Basque cheesecake with a deeply caramelized dark top and creamy pale center on a wooden board
ingredients: Unsalted butter, softened, for the pan
32 oz full-fat brick cream cheese, at room temperature
2 cups heavy cream, at room temperature

instructions.name: Prepare the tall parchment collar
instructions.text: Heat the oven to 425°F with a rack in the center. Lightly butter a 9-inch springform pan. Crumple two 16-inch sheets of parchment, smooth them out, and overlap them inside the pan so they cover the base and extend at least 3 inches above the rim. Press the folds against the sides and set the pan on a rimmed sheet pan.

instructions.name: Smooth the cream cheese base
instructions.text: Beat the room-temperature cream cheese, sugar, and salt in a large bowl with an electric mixer on medium-low for 2 to 3 minutes, scraping the bowl twice, until completely smooth. Keep the speed moderate; incorporating excessive air can make the cake puff and crack dramatically.

instructions.name: Add the eggs gradually
instructions.text: Beat in the eggs one at a time on low speed, mixing each only until no yellow streaks remain and scraping after the third egg. The batter should be glossy and lump-free before the cream is added.

instructions.name: Finish without flour pockets
instructions.text: Mix in the heavy cream, vanilla, and lemon zest on low. Sift the flour over the batter and mix just until incorporated, about 20 seconds. Scrape the bottom with a flexible spatula and stir by hand six to eight times. Pour into the lined pan and tap it firmly on the counter three times to release large bubbles.

instructions.name: Bake to a bronzed, safe center
instructions.text: Bake at 425°F for 50 to 55 minutes. The top should be deep mahogany, the outer 2 inches set, and the center should wobble as one soft mass rather than ripple like liquid. Check through the side of the center with an instant-read thermometer: it should register 155 to 160°F and reach at least 160°F with carryover heat. If the top darkens before the center is ready, loosely shield only the darkest area with foil.

instructions.name: Cool in stages
instructions.text: Cool the cheesecake in its pan on a rack for 2 hours; it will sink and form the characteristic rumpled edge. Cover without touching the surface and refrigerate for at least 4 hours, preferably overnight. The realistic start-to-slice time is about 7 hours, including 25 minutes prep, 55 minutes baking, 2 hours cooling, and 4 hours chilling.

instructions.name: Unmold and slice cleanly
instructions.text: Release the springform ring, peel the parchment down from the sides, and let the cake stand at room temperature for 20 minutes. Cut with a long thin knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between slices. Serve plain so the caramelized top and vanilla-lemon custard stay the focus.

why_it_works: Room-temperature dairy blends before too much air is incorporated, producing a custardy interior instead of visible cream-cheese pellets.
High heat rapidly caramelizes the exposed top while the tall parchment collar protects the tender, crustless sides.
A staged room-temperature cool followed by a full chill lets the loose center set cleanly without sacrificing its soft texture.
swaps: Use orange zest instead of lemon for a warmer citrus note, keeping the quantity at 2 teaspoons so the custard is not overwhelmed.
For a gluten-free cake, replace the flour with 30 g cornstarch; sift it carefully because cornstarch clumps easily.
Do not substitute tub-style spreadable cream cheese, light cream cheese, or half-and-half; their water and stabilizer levels change both browning and set.
storage: Refrigerate tightly covered for up to 5 days. For the cleanest slices, cut only what you need and return the cake promptly to the refrigerator. Freeze individual slices, double-wrapped, for up to 1 month; thaw overnight in the refrigerator. Basque cheesecake is best served cool or after 20 minutes at room temperature and should not be reheated.
notes: The full timeline is about 7 hours, but active preparation is only 25 minutes. Overnight chilling gives the most reliable slices.
A pale top means the oven ran cool or the cake was removed early; the dark caramelized surface is intentional, but it should smell toasted rather than acrid.
Place the springform pan on a rimmed sheet pan to catch butter or batter seepage; the sheet pan also makes the tall parchment-lined pan easier to move.

faqs.q: Why did my cheesecake crack and sink?
faqs.a: Both are normal for Basque cheesecake. The batter puffs in the hot oven and settles as steam escapes, creating the rustic folds. Avoiding excess mixer speed limits very large fissures, but a flat New York-style surface is not the goal.

faqs.q: How dark should the top really be?
faqs.a: Aim for deep mahogany with a few nearly black patches, not an evenly charcoal surface. Begin checking at 48 minutes and use the center temperature and wobble—rather than color alone—to decide when it is done.

faqs.q: Can I bake it in a regular cake pan?
faqs.a: Yes, if it is 9 inches wide and at least 3 inches deep. Line it generously with overlapping parchment and chill the cake fully before using the paper as a sling; a springform is easier and safer for unmolding.
